items.title: 71231_Sam Wooding Oral History Interview
items.q: And at that time in wa-wa Harlem was stuck on jungle music and the wow-wow with Johnny Dunn, Tommy Morris, Bubba Miley, and Charley Evers

ctx.x: band, they said, 'Well, we'll let you go. But you'd better be ready when you come in here, or out you go on your nose.' See, so anyhow, we opened up. And the time come and we opened up with this band, and the first note we hit, we thought it was good. But nobody danced. Well, I was scared to death. I thought it was because they didn't like it. Well, this was the beginning of concert, and I didn't realize that. For jazz bands. Then we went through the whole set. And everybody, when we got through playing, then…

Well, I wasn't trying for a sound, I was trying to eat, as I said before. You see, so it worked out. And from then on, now we're starting to have, people are starting to come in and wouldn't do very little dancing. We had to resort to such things like the blues and some of the little pop numbers in order to get them to dance. Because they were so sitting listening (unintelligible), and I had tried something new. I had tried using augmented chords, which gave it a sort of foreign effect. And at that time in wa-wa…

the one thing quiet as it's kept. That's the one thing that made Duke Ellington. The wa-wa and the plunger thing which he took from Bubber Miley, and he made a classic out of it. He using it with the whole band, but it really started - turned it into something by (unintelligible) Johnny Dunn was the first one. This Johnny Dunn, later on, worked with Mamie Smith and I guess Bessie Smith and Clara Smith and everybody else. But Johnny Dunn, he ended up with Lew Leslie, playing for Florence Mills, you see?
